carcinogen.help: IARC Group 1 means carcinogenic to humans, Group 2A probably carcinogenic. EU Carc. 1A means known, 1B presumed to cause cancer in humans. These describe a hazard, not the risk at the amount in one product.
carcinogen.label: Classified as a known or probable human carcinogen

carcinogen-possible.help: IARC Group 2B means possibly carcinogenic to humans. EU Carc. 2 means suspected human carcinogen. These describe a hazard, not the risk at the amount in one product.
carcinogen-possible.label: Classified as a possible or suspected human carcinogen

csc.help: The Campaign for Safe Cosmetics is an advocacy group. Its profiles explain why it considers these ingredients a concern.
csc.label: Listed as a chemical of concern by the Campaign for Safe Cosmetics

endocrine.help: EU ED List I: substances identified as endocrine (hormone) disruptors under EU law.
endocrine.label: Identified as an endocrine disruptor at EU level (ED List I)

endocrine-eval.help: EU ED List II: under evaluation as an endocrine disruptor in an EU process. List III: identified as one by a national authority in the EU.
endocrine-eval.label: Under EU evaluation as an endocrine disruptor, or identified as one by a national authority (ED Lists II and III)

evidence.text: The EU bans more than 1,400 substances from cosmetics, while US rules restrict only a handful.
evidence.tip: Moderate evidence · Review of other studies

eu-banned.help: Annex II of the EU Cosmetics Regulation lists substances that must not be used in cosmetics sold in the EU.
eu-banned.label: Prohibited in cosmetics in the EU

eu-restricted.help: Annex III (restricted substances) or Annex V (preservatives) of the EU Cosmetics Regulation sets maximum amounts, allowed product types or required warnings.
eu-restricted.label: Allowed in EU cosmetics only with limits

formaldehyde.help: These preservatives slowly release formaldehyde into the product. The EU classifies formaldehyde as a carcinogen and a skin sensitizer, and requires a “releases formaldehyde” warning above a set level.
formaldehyde.label: Formaldehyde-releasing preservative

ifra-partial.help: IFRA, the fragrance industry's own standards body, prohibits this material in some forms and sets limits on others. The linked standard says which.
ifra-partial.label: Prohibited in some forms, limited in others, by the fragrance industry's own IFRA standard
ifra-partial.short: Partly banned by the fragrance industry

evidence.text: The fragrance industry's safety system is self-run: by its own 2003 description, companies fund the Research Institute for Fragrance Materials through dues, its expert panel reviews ingredient safety, and conclusions go to the industry's trade body IFRA, which sets voluntary standards for those same companies. No regulator appears in the loop.
evidence.tip: Strong evidence · Review of other studies

ifra-prohibited.help: IFRA is the fragrance industry's own standards body. Its standards are voluntary; a prohibition means the IFRA standard says not to use the substance in fragrance.
ifra-prohibited.label: Prohibited by the fragrance industry's own IFRA standard
ifra-prohibited.short: Banned by the fragrance industry itself

ifra-restricted.help: IFRA, the fragrance industry's own standards body, sets maximum amounts for this material in different kinds of products.
ifra-restricted.label: Use limited by the fragrance industry's own IFRA standard

leave-on-banned.help: EU rules allow this ingredient only in products you wash off. It isn't allowed in creams, lotions, makeup or other products left on the skin.
leave-on-banned.label: The EU allows it only in rinse-off products (like shampoo or soap), not in leave-on products (like lotion or makeup)
leave-on-banned.short: Not allowed in EU leave-on products

mutagen.help: EU Muta. 1A or 1B: may cause genetic defects.
mutagen.label: Classified as able to cause genetic defects

mutagen-suspected.help: EU Muta. 2: suspected of causing genetic defects.
mutagen-suspected.label: Classified as suspected of causing genetic defects

evidence.text: Many fragrance chemicals become stronger skin allergens after the bottle is opened: limonene, linalool and geraniol react with air at room temperature to form hydroperoxides that, in mouse tests, sensitize at 5-10 times lower concentrations than the fresh chemical.

oxidizes.help: These scent chemicals react with air once a product is opened and form hydroperoxides, which are much stronger skin allergens. See the graded evidence below.
oxidizes.label: Reacts with air to form stronger skin allergens

evidence.text: Since the 2022 MoCRA law, most cosmetic makers must list their products with the FDA; in its December 2025 report the FDA found PFAS ("forever chemicals") intentionally added to about 0.4% of listed US cosmetics (1,744 of 430,134), mostly eye and face makeup, and had too little data to judge the safety of 19 of the 25 most-used PFAS.
evidence.tip: Strong evidence · Review of other studies

pfas.help: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, nicknamed “forever chemicals”. We flag ingredient names that mark a fluorinated chemical.
pfas.label: PFAS, the “forever chemicals”

reprotoxic.help: EU Repr. 1A or 1B: may damage fertility or the unborn child.
reprotoxic.label: Classified as a reproductive toxicant (may damage fertility or the unborn child)

reprotoxic-suspected.help: EU Repr. 2: suspected of damaging fertility or the unborn child.
reprotoxic-suspected.label: Classified as suspected of damaging fertility or the unborn child

resp-sensitizer.help: EU hazard statement H334: may cause allergy or asthma symptoms or breathing difficulties if inhaled.
resp-sensitizer.label: Classified as a respiratory sensitizer (may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled)

scent-ingredient.help: The EU ingredient database (CosIng) lists this ingredient's function as perfuming or fragrance, so it may be there to add scent, even on a label that never says “fragrance.”
scent-ingredient.label: Used to add scent: its official function is perfuming or fragrance

evidence.text: In a survey of 187 US pediatric personal-care products, preservatives (57.8% of products) were a more common source of contact allergens than fragrance (29.4%), even though the products were being screened specifically for hypoallergenic/fragrance-related marketing claims.
evidence.tip: Moderate evidence · Measured in people or real products

skin-sensitizer.help: EU hazard statement H317: may cause an allergic skin reaction.
skin-sensitizer.label: Classified as a skin sensitizer (may cause an allergic skin reaction)

limits: Contaminants are never on the label. 1,4-dioxane, for example, can form when ingredients are made and won’t be listed.
“Fragrance” can hide dozens of chemicals we can’t see, including some on these lists.
We can’t see how much of an ingredient is in the product. A classification describes a hazard, not the risk from one product.
Names on real labels vary. If an ingredient isn’t flagged, it may be spelled differently from the lists we use.
We check EU and international lists. US law bans far fewer ingredients, so a product sold legally in the US can still contain something banned in the EU.
